newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-CLARKE OWES MUCH TO MONTGOMERIE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-CLARKE OWES MUCH TO MONTGOMERIE.

text.p: If Darren Clarke goes on to win the British Open at Royal Troon this weekend, he will owe a huge vote of thanks to the home town favourite, local boy Colin Montgomerie.
For it was Montgomerie who offered his good friend Clarke a lot of advice when they played practice rounds together early in the week.
Clarke opened a two-shot lead over the field on Friday after rounds of 67-66 with world number four Montgomerie mired in a share of 40th place.
"I played with Monty on Monday and Wednesday and he gave me a lot of advice about Troon because I hadn't played it before this week," the burly Northern Irishman said.
"He told me certain areas where not to go, what shots not to take on, what side to miss the green on, that sort of thing."
"With the way he was playing and the way I was playing, I may have expected our positions to be the other way around, but that's golf," he said.
For his part, Montgomerie is delighted that if he is not leading, Clarke is.
"I think I gave him too much help this week but I am delighted he is ahead because we are firm friends.
"He has more talent in his left pinkie than most European Tour players. He has always had great potential and hopefully he can now show it.
"I wish him all the best. What he has to do now is play his game, not worry about his position and not look at leaderboards too much," the Scot said.
Talented but inconsistent would be an apt description of Clarke before this year, for the words promising and potential have been bandied in his direction for several years.
"My consistency seems to be improving. I am getting into contention more than I used to," Clarke said.
Though he has only two victories under his belt and has not won this year, Clarke has a second, two thirds and two fourths to his credit in 1997.
He believes his improvement has stemmed from controlling his aggression.
"I think I'm probably more aggressive at the right times now. For example, I'm trying to play short of the bunkers here instead of trying to clear them as I might have done a year ago."
"I don't get as annoyed with myself when I hit shots I don't like," he said.
He is assured of a Ryder Cup debut for Europe against the Americans at Valderrama in September and is on a nice little offer from his sponsors if he is successful.
"They have offered me a new Ferrari if I play at least two matches and am undefeated," he said.

Clarke, 29 next month, comes from Dungannon in Northern Ireland and when he scored his first tour victory in the 1993 Belgian Open he phoned home to set up a free bar for the members at his local golf club.
It cost him about 1,000 pounds ($1,670).
"If I win here on Sunday, it will be a bigger party than that," he said.
